title: Banjoists after 1949 and the WPA
summary: He names banjoists active when he returned, explains why he skipped the WPA band, and says he is freelancing.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: Yeah. Can you remember any other banjo players, when you got back to New Orleans, you know, when you got back the final time that impressed you? Yeah. About 56, who else was playing around about then?
Well, when you got back into New Orleans.

Yeah, well, I got back in Chicago in 49. Yeah. Oh, yeah, Halston Verrett, he was still playing. George Gino was still playing. Mm-hmm. And, uh, uh, Fred Miner, we call him H.A. Miner, was still playing the banjo. And, uh, see, that's all. There was a terrific guy around here in the 30s, was named Penn. Mm-hmm. He was another terrific picker, but I think he had, he had died somewhere in, uh, in the 40s, I think. Mm-hmm. I think it was our late 40s, like that, or maybe the early 50.
He was with the WPA band, all the musicians, remember. You know, he probably wouldn't have told no more. Yeah, yeah. He was a terrific picker, yeah.
You weren't with the WPA at all, wasn't he?

No, I didn't go because I could always do better without the WPA. I mean, I was working with bands like Sidney and Poulon, and I had other guys I'd be working with when, uh, the big band wouldn't be working, you know? But, like, this time of year, say, from the holiday, Christmas holidays, and to Mardi Gras, man, we'd be busy. Yeah. Only time we'd have a break was after, uh, Mardi Gras, between Mardi Gras and during the Lent, see? Mm-hmm. And those days.
And, uh, you were just, like, gigging around now, you know? I mean, you were just freelancing now?
Well, that's what I'm doing here. I'd plan with bands like that.
